intro: In 2011 a five-century lime standing before the village church in Leliceni, in Transylvania's Szekler hills, was voted European Tree of the Year with 23,298 votes, the biggest margin the contest has produced. Villagers are said to have ringed its trunk with log benches and settled local business under its crown, a tradition some say continues today. Local tradition also holds that the tree and the church survived a Tatar raid that burned the surrounding village, though no source documents when. Harghita county declared it a natural monument in 1992.

question_answer: Leliceni's notable tree is the Lime Tree of Leliceni, a Small-leaved Lime standing in front of the village's Roman Catholic church, roughly 500 years old and 3.9 metres round, voted European Tree of the Year in 2011.
question_context: The tree's real claim is civic rather than botanical. By local tradition, villagers ringed the trunk with log benches and sat under the crown to argue out the affairs of the village, and wooden benches are said to stand there still, which makes it something closer to a parish meeting room than an ordinary churchyard tree. It won Romania's own national tree contest before going on to take European Tree of the Year in 2011 with 23,298 votes, the largest winning margin the contest has produced in any year checked so far. Harghita county declared it a natural monument the following year, in 1992. Local tradition also holds that the tree and the church beside it survived a Tatar raid that burned the surrounding village, though the sources that repeat this place it anywhere across the 1600s and none of them documents the event, so it stands as the story the village tells rather than as settled history. The most recent confirmation found dates from the contest years around 2011 and 2012; nothing more recent has surfaced.

trees.story:
In 2011 a lime in front of a village church in the Szekler hills of Transylvania was voted European Tree of the Year, with 23,298 votes. It had won Romania's own contest first. Leliceni, Csíkszentlélek in Hungarian, sits a few kilometres north of Miercurea Ciuc, and the tree has stood before its Roman Catholic church for roughly five hundred years: the contest and Romanian national news both date its planting to the early 1500s. It is about 20 metres tall and 3.9 metres round, and the county declared it a natural monument in 1992.

Its real claim is civic rather than botanical. By local tradition the villagers ringed the trunk with log benches and sat under the crown to argue out the affairs of the village, and wooden benches are said to stand there still. A tree that has served as the parish meeting room for centuries has heard more local politics than most town halls.

Local tradition also says the tree and the church came through a Tatar raid that burned the village around them. Sources place that raid at various points in the 1600s and none documents it, so take it as the story the village tells rather than as history.

The most recent reports we have found date from the contest years, around 2011 and 2012. If you have stood under it since, tell us how it is doing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its place directly in front of the village's Roman Catholic church and by a trunk 3.9 metres round. It is the big lime in the churchyard.

best_time.label: early July, when the lime flowers and the churchyard smells sweet
